read: full (main text pp.1-9 and appendix A.1-A.6 on pp.13-15 read; supplementary figures and module lists on pp.16-22 not read)
venue_now: NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (p.1 footer); the May reference list prints it as an arXiv preprint
what_it_is: MATH is 12,500 competition mathematics problems (AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME and others; 7,500 train, 5,000 test) in seven subjects, with difficulty levels 1 to 5 (p.4). Each problem has a full step-by-step LaTeX solution and a boxed final answer (pp.1, 4). Models are scored by exact match of the boxed answer after normalisation rules (p.5). The paper also releases AMPS, a pretraining corpus of Khan Academy problems and about 5 million problems generated by 100 Mathematica scripts (pp.2, 5-6). GPT-2 and GPT-3 models reach 3.0% to 6.9% (p.2).
size: 12,500 problems (7,500 train, 5,000 test) (p.4); models: GPT-2 0.1B-1.5B and GPT-3 13B and 175B (Table 2, p.5)
source_of_items: competitions (AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME and more, many collected from AoPS) (p.4)
instances: static (the benchmark); only the separate AMPS pretraining corpus is partly generated by Mathematica scripts (pp.5-6)
has_gold_traces: partial: every problem has a full step-by-step solution in LaTeX and natural language (pp.1, 4); the solutions are used for training and as hints (p.9), never to score a model's steps
evaluation: final answer: exact match of the boxed answer after normalisation rules (equivalent fractions, ordering of factors, optional units) (p.5)
human_validation: No item validation is reported beyond the competition source (p.4). A rough human-performance study gave 20 test problems to six university students, four of them authors; scores ranged from 40% to 90% (pp.5, 15). The answer checker is not validated against human grading.
contamination_measures: none (problems come from public competition archives, p.4)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-M1 (L155-161): 'In mathematics, benchmarks ranging from GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and Math (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) to HardMath (Fan et al., 2024), Putnam-Axiom (Gulati et al., 2024), and GSM-Symbolic (Mirzadeh et al., 2024) rigorously test abstract logical deduction and reasoning stability.' AND S-I3b (L105-111): 'specialized benchmarks (e.g., Math (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) or HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021)) assess abstract logic and algorithmic translation.'
engtrace_use.explanation: S-M1: MATH is competition mathematics, framed as measuring problem solving with heuristics ('analyze a problem, pick out good heuristics ... and chain them together'), as opposed to plug-and-chug calculation (pp.1, 4). It scores only the boxed final answer by exact match (p.5). Its own examples show a model giving 'the right answer yet ... a misleading and wrong explanation' (p.7, Fig. 3), so 'rigorously test ... deduction' overstates what is checked. It also has no stability or perturbation component for the 'reasoning stability' half to describe. S-I3b, 'assess abstract logic', is acceptable as an introduction-level gloss on a specialised mathematics benchmark without physical grounding. Neither use is wrong; S-M1 is loose, and the field records the less favourable of the two verdicts.

suggested_wording: MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) collects 12,500 competition problems, each with a full step-by-step solution, but scores only the boxed final answer by exact match.
facts_to_cite: 12,500 problems from mathematics competitions (AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME), split 7,500 train and 5,000 test (p.4)
Each problem has a full step-by-step solution and a boxed final answer (pp.1, 4)
Scoring is exact match of the boxed final answer after normalisation (p.5)
Models can give the right answer with a misleading and wrong explanation (p.7, Fig. 3)
Having GPT-2 1.5B generate step-by-step solutions before answering lowered accuracy, to 5.3% (p.9)
Published in the NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (p.1)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: a worked step-by-step solution for every problem (p.4); deterministic answer checking with explicit equivalence rules (p.5), as EngTrace's answer check does with its tolerance; difficulty levels (p.4), loosely like EngTrace's tiers. Lacks: generated instances (static, from public competitions, p.4); step-level evaluation (boxed answer only, p.5); an engineering or physical domain; expert validation of the evaluator; any contamination measure.
notes: MATH already pairs every problem with a full step-by-step solution (p.4), as GSM8K does (Cobbe et al., p.3). EngTrace cannot claim novelty for pairing instances with reference solutions as such, only for generating a computed trace per instance and scoring steps against it. The May reference list gives MATH as an arXiv preprint; the text shows NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks (p.1). If the duplicate MMLU entries (Hendrycks 2020 and 2021a) are merged, this key's '2021b' suffix changes (citation_context_map C5). The Fig. 3 example (p.7) is usable motivation for the process-supervision paragraph.
